primary_text_note: Golding 1954 is in copyright and no text was available under scripts/_retrofc/_texts/. Every quotation was checked by web search against sources that reproduce Golding's wording (SparkNotes, Shmoop, eNotes, CliffsNotes, americanliterature.com). Quotations are only flagged below where the real wording was found.

findings.claim: KC[0] "Which assessment objectives are tested in the Paper 2 Section A essay on modern texts?" is keyed to option 2, "AO1, AO3, and AO4 (SPaG)".
findings.truth: AQA 8702 Paper 2 Section A assesses AO1, AO2, AO3 and AO4. The keyed answer denies AO2 outright, and AO2 is worth 12 of the 30 marks (AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6, plus 4 AO4). No option in the list was right: option 1 drops AO3, option 3 ("All four AOs equally") is wrong because the AOs are not weighted equally. A student who learns this key would leave language, form and structure out of the essay and cap themselves at about half marks. FIX: option 2 becomes "AO1, AO2, AO3 and AO4 (SPaG)" (key stays at index 2) and option 3 becomes "AO2 and AO4 (SPaG) only" so there is one right answer.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md - section 2 (Paper 2: Modern texts and poetry; Section A one essay from a choice of two), section 4.1 AO list, section 4.2 Paper 2 AO weightings (AO1 22.5 / AO2 27.5 / AO3 7.5 / AO4 2.5 of the GCSE). Also the unit's own exam tip, which states 30 marks + 4 SPaG.

findings.claim: "Golding describes Jack looking at his reflection: ... The paint frees Jack ..." quotes the mask as making him “safe from shame or self-consciousness”.
findings.truth: Golding's wording in Chapter 4 is “the mask was a thing on its own, behind which Jack hid, liberated from shame and self-consciousness”. “Safe from shame or self-consciousness” is not in the novel. This is one of the six quotations the unit tells students to memorise, so the wrong wording would be reproduced verbatim in a closed-book essay.
findings.evidence: https://www.shmoop.com/quotes/liberated-from-shame-and-self-consciousness.html and https://www.sparknotes.com/lit/flies/quotes/theme/the-dangers-of-mob-mentality/ - both give the Chapter 4 sentence in full.

findings.claim: Flashcard [1] “What does Jack's face paint symbolically allow?” → “He becomes 'safe from shame or self-consciousness'”.
findings.truth: Same misquotation as F2. The flashcard is the memorisation surface, so it matters more than the prose.

findings.claim: "they “wedged” themselves on top of her, and Roger drives his spear “right up her ass.”"
findings.truth: Two errors in one sentence. (1) The quoted word is not “wedged”: Golding writes that the hunters followed the sow “wedded to her in lust, excited by the long chase and the dropped blood”. “Wedded” is the whole point of the line, and it is the word examiners expect. (2) “Right up her ass!” is Robert's line, not Roger's - Robert shouts it as a joke about where Roger's spear went. Attributing a quotation to the wrong speaker is a standard mark-loser.
findings.evidence: https://www.enotes.com/topics/lord-of-the-flies/questions/analysis-killing-sow-scene-lord-of-the-flies-593861 (“wedded to her in lust”) and https://rcs-10h-lord-of-the-flies.fandom.com/wiki/Chapter_8 (“Robert stabilized the thing in a phrase which was received uproariously: 'Right up her ass!'”).

findings.claim: practice_questions[2].marks: "... and the littluns' cruelty (Roger throwing stones, Henry torturing creatures)".
findings.truth: Roger is not a littlun. He is one of the older boys - a member of Jack's choir and later his hunters - and the stones in Chapter 4 are thrown at Henry, who is the littlun. The mark scheme as written invites a student to write that Roger is one of the little ones, which contradicts this unit's own Roger material in L5 and L6.
findings.evidence: Chapter 4: Roger throws stones round Henry, keeping a six-yard space he dare not throw into; Chapter 11: Roger levers the rock that kills Piggy. Both are established in this unit's L5 content.

findings.claim: "Third, and most devastating: the officer is standing on the deck of a warship."
findings.truth: The officer is standing on the beach in front of Ralph; his ship is offshore. Golding's final sentence has him turn away and rest his eyes on “the trim cruiser in the distance”. The irony the paragraph is making is real, but the staging is wrong, and a student repeating it would misdescribe the closing scene.
findings.evidence: Chapter 12, closing paragraph (“... and waited, allowing his eyes to rest on the trim cruiser in the distance”) - https://www.sparknotes.com/lit/flies/quotes/character/ralph/

findings.claim: All 42 practice questions across the 7 lessons carry the type label “30+4 marks — Shakespeare Essay”.
findings.truth: Lord of the Flies is a modern prose text: AQA 8702 section 3.2.1, examined in Paper 2 Section A as one essay from a choice of two, closed book, no extract. It is not on Paper 1 and it is not a Shakespeare play. The mark totals (30 + 4 SPaG) are correct, so the fix is the label alone. The sibling AQA modern-text unit blood-brothers had the identical fault and was relabelled “30+4 marks — Modern Text Essay”, which this unit now matches.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md section 3.2.1 (Prose: William Golding, Lord of the Flies) and section 2 (Paper 2 Section A). Precedent: scripts/_retrofc/units/english-literature-aqa__blood-brothers/_report.json.

findings.claim: 41 of the 42 practice questions print a broken band ladder: “Top band (26-30)”, “Upper band (21-25)”, “Top band (16-20)”, “Upper-mid band (11-15)”, “Lower-mid band (6-10)”, “Lower band (1-5)”. “Top band” appears twice and “Mid band” is missing.
findings.truth: The mark ranges are right; only the names are wrong, and the repair is deterministic: within each affected marks string, “Top band (16-20)” becomes “Upper-mid band (16-20)” and “Upper-mid band (11-15)” becomes “Mid band (11-15)”. That yields the six-label ladder this unit's own L1 Q1 already uses (Top 26-30 / Upper 21-25 / Upper-mid 16-20 / Mid 11-15 / Lower-mid 6-10 / Lower 1-5). OPTIONS: (a) route to the standing 178-band-ladder workstream, which is what I recommend - the rename is mechanical, identical across 41 strings, and the same fault runs through other AQA units, so one pass should own it; (b) rewrite all 41 marks strings here, which duplicates that workstream and puts 41 long whole-string edits through this unit's apply run for a labelling change; (c) leave as is, which I do not recommend, because a student reads “Top band” against a 16-20 mark answer.

findings.claim: “The novel's final image is Ralph weeping” (repeated in flashcard [14], “What is the final image of Lord of the Flies?”).
findings.truth: Ralph's weeping is in the final paragraph, but Golding's last clause moves to the officer looking out at “the trim cruiser in the distance” - which is the sharper AO2 point, because the book closes on the warship rather than on the boy. Not wrong enough to edit, and an edit here would force a re-narration for no gain in marks.

summary: Seven lessons checked against the 8702 spec and web sources for the in-copyright text; 9 findings, 49 edits written (2 HIGH families, 5 MEDIUM one-off fixes, 1 ADJUDICATE, 1 NOTE). The one that costs real marks is L7's knowledge check on assessment objectives, which marked an AO2-denying option as correct on a paper where AO2 is worth 12 of 30. Two quotations were fabricated or garbled - Jack's mask is “liberated from shame and self-consciousness”, not “safe from”, and the sow hunt is “wedded to her in lust”, not “wedged” - and “Right up her ass!” is Robert's line, not Roger's. Everything else held: chapter numbers and titles, the deaths of the birthmarked boy (ch. 2), Simon (ch. 9) and Piggy (ch. 11), the forty-foot fall, the conch's “thousand white fragments”, Ralph's final tricolon, the Coral Island frame, Piggy's atom-bomb line in ch. 1, and every knowledge-check and flashcard key except the AO question. Lessons 1, 2 and 6 carry no unit-specific fault; the label and band-ladder findings are fleet-wide, not theirs.
